name: Old Indian Defense
summary: The Old Indian Defense (1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6) is a solid, restrained cousin of the King's Indian aiming for ...e5.
intro: The Old Indian Defense arises after 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6, a compact and unhurried system in which Black stakes out the center with a later ...e5 rather than an immediate confrontation. It is the older, more restrained cousin of the King's Indian Defence: the same central idea, but with the king's bishop developed modestly to e7 instead of being fianchettoed on g7. The result is a resilient, low-maintenance setup that trades sharp theory for sound, flexible piece play.

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: Black's central ambition is the ...e5 break, supported by pawns on d6 and e5 and pieces developed behind them, typically ...Nbd7, ...Be7, ...O-O and ...c6. Because the dark-squared bishop stays on e7 rather than g7, Black accepts a slightly more passive, cramped game in exchange for a durable structure and fewer forcing lines to memorize. Once ...e5 is achieved, the position takes on a King's-Indian character, and Black looks for gradual regrouping, well-timed pawn breaks such as ...exd4 or ...c6 followed by ...d5, and pressure against White's center.

White, for his part, enjoys more space and easier development, and usually completes the natural build-up with Nc3, Nf3, e4 and a harmonious deployment of the bishops. The strategic battle revolves around whether White can exploit the extra room and the tempo Black spends preparing ...e5, or whether Black can neutralize the space with timely exchanges and reach a comfortable, solid middlegame. Both sides must watch the tension in the center: releasing it too early can hand the opponent a favorable structure or open lines.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: After 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6, White's most principled continuation is 3.Nc3, when Black plays 3...e5, striking in the center at once. The main line runs 4.Nf3 Nbd7 (defending e5 and preparing to recapture toward the center), reaching the classical tabiya where White can maintain the tension, play 5.e4 to build a broad pawn center, or clarify matters with 5.dxe5. A key alternative for Black is to meet an early exchange on e5 by recapturing with a knight or pawn depending on the resulting piece activity.

White also has quieter and independent tries, including the fianchetto approach with g3 and Bg2, and setups with Bg5 pinning the f6-knight to pressure the ...e5 break. Transpositions are common: the Old Indian frequently blends into King's Indian, Czech-style ...c6 structures, or even Philidor-like formations, so understanding the pawn skeletons matters more than rote memorization. In every case the thematic question is the same, namely how and when Black executes ...e5 and whether the ensuing exchanges favor his more compact camp.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The Old Indian is closely associated with Mikhail Chigorin, whose classical, piece-oriented approach to the ...d6 and ...e5 setup gave the opening its enduring identity, and it was later refined and championed by a number of Soviet practitioners who valued its solidity. As the sharper King's Indian Defence rose to prominence in the twentieth century, this earlier treatment came to be known as the Old Indian, a dependable weapon for players who prefer sound structure and gradual maneuvering over immediate tactical complications.

keyIdeas: Reach the ...e5 break from a compact, King's-Indian-like structure.
Develop the king's bishop modestly to e7 rather than fianchettoing on g7.
Trade sharp theory for a solid, low-maintenance setup.
Support the center with ...Nbd7, ...Be7, ...O-O and often ...c6.
Accept slight passivity and space in return for structural resilience.
Time exchanges like ...exd4 or ...c6 and ...d5 to free the position.

white: Build a broad center with Nc3, Nf3 and e4, using the extra space.
Maintain central tension to pressure Black's cramped setup.
Consider the fianchetto with g3 and Bg2 for a positional grip.
Try Bg5 to pin the f6-knight and complicate the ...e5 break.
Exploit Black's spent tempi with well-timed piece activity.
black: Prepare and execute the freeing ...e5 break behind ...Nbd7 and ...Be7.
Complete development with ...O-O and a solid ...c6 or ...c5.
Relieve the cramp through timely exchanges such as ...exd4.
Aim for ...c6 and ...d5 to challenge White's center directly.
Reroute pieces gradually toward active squares after castling.
